hook: A meadow has 364 purple flowers and 36 white ones. How many of the purple plants secretly carry a white allele? You cannot tell by looking, but if the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, two short equations on the formula sheet tell you: 168. The same arithmetic estimates how many people carry the allele for a recessive disorder.

prereq.q: In p² + 2pq + q² = 1, what does 2pq stand for?
options: The frequency of the dominant allele
The frequency of homozygous recessive individuals
prereq.why: p² is homozygous dominant, 2pq heterozygous and q² homozygous recessive.

prereq.q: Which condition is NOT required for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
prereq.why: Equilibrium needs a very large population (no drift), random mating, no selection, no mutation and no gene flow.

prereq.q: A chi-square value greater than the critical value means you…
options: fail to reject the null hypothesis
prereq.why: A large χ² means the observed counts are too far from expected for chance.

figure.caption: With p = 0.7 and q = 0.3, the areas give genotype frequencies: p² = 0.49, 2pq = 0.42, q² = 0.09. Start from q²: it is the one genotype you can read straight from phenotypes.

chain.cause: Only the recessive phenotype has a single genotype (aa).
chain.effect: Its frequency equals q² at equilibrium: 36 white of 400 gives q² = 0.09.

chain.cause: Taking the square root undoes the squaring.
Random union of alleles gives genotypes in proportions p², 2pq and q².
chain.effect: Heterozygotes are 2pq = 0.42 of the population: 168 of 400 plants.

chain.cause: If you know all genotype counts, you can count alleles directly and calculate expected counts.
chain.effect: A chi-square test compares observed and expected genotypes and shows whether the population departs from equilibrium.

chain.cause: Allele frequencies measured at two times differ.
chain.effect: The change in p or q is evidence that something (selection, drift, gene flow) is acting on the population.

ideas: Worked example. 36 white of 400 plants. q² = 36 ÷ 400 = 0.09; q = 0.30; p = 0.70. Expected AA = 0.49 × 400 = 196; Aa = 0.42 × 400 = 168; aa = 36.
Never take the dominant phenotype frequency as p: purple plants (0.91) are AA plus Aa. Always start from the recessive class.
With genotype counts, count alleles: p = (2 × AA + Aa) ÷ (2 × total). Then expected counts are p²N, 2pqN and q²N.
Rare recessive alleles hide in carriers: at q = 0.02, carriers (2pq ≈ 0.039) outnumber affected people (q² = 0.0004) about 98 to 1.

misconception.wrong: The frequency of the dominant allele is the fraction of the population showing the dominant phenotype.
misconception.right: Dominant-phenotype individuals include heterozygotes, so their fraction is p² + 2pq, not p. Find q from the recessive class first (q² = recessive frequency), then p = 1 − q.

summary: For a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the recessive phenotype frequency is q², so q = √(recessive frequency) and p = 1 − q. Genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q², and 2pq is the carrier frequency. With full genotype counts, count alleles to get p and use a chi-square test to check whether the population fits equilibrium. A change in allele frequency between generations is evidence of evolution.
